text: Bias doesn't come from the algorithm, overwhelmingly it comes from the data a model is trained on, before any algorithm is involved. This lesson goes one level deeper into the four specific ways it enters.

Historical bias, the data accurately reflects past decisions that were themselves unequal, a model learns to repeat the pattern, not correct it. Sampling bias, the training population doesn't match the population the model will actually serve, a direct consequence of the completeness dimension from last lesson. Measurement bias, the data uses a proxy that doesn't mean the same thing for everyone. Label bias, when humans assign the labels, their own judgments and inconsistencies become the ground truth the model treats as objectively correct.

A model can score well on overall accuracy while performing meaningfully worse for a specific subgroup, because the overall number averages across everyone. That's exactly why bias testing has to look at subgroup performance specifically, a single accuracy score can hide exactly the problem governance exists to catch.

Catching bias in the data means asking the representation and proxy questions before training. Does this training population resemble the population the model will serve? Are known historical inequities baked into this data's outcomes? Is any variable standing in for something it shouldn't? None of these require advanced statistics, they require someone assigned to ask them and document the answer, before the data is approved for training.
A learning algorithm finds and reinforces patterns already present in what it's shown. Next up: data labeling and governance, where label bias gets its full treatment.
